Crashworthiness Performance Evaluation of Thin-Walled Tubes Filled with Single and 
Hybrid-Lattice Structures Under Axial Impact Loading Using Finite Element Analysis 
Mahmoud Sultan1* 
, Anwar Kandil1 
, and Mohamed Baraya1 
 
 
1Department of Production Engineering and Mechanical Design, Faculty of Engineering, Port Said University, Port Fouad, Egypt 
 
This study aims to evaluate the crashworthiness performance of hybrid energy-absorbing structures 
composed of thin-walled square tubes filled with various lattice configurations. The research seeks to 
determine how combining different lattice types (single, dual-hybrid, and triple-hybrid) affects energy 
absorption under axial impact loading, contributing to the development of lightweight and high-per-
formance crashworthy systems for transportation safety. Finite Element Analysis (FEA) was per-
formed using Abaqus/Explicit to simulate axial impact loading on hybrid models. Each model con-
sisted of a thin-walled square aluminum tube (Al6063-T5) filled with an internal lattice structure 
(AlSi10Mg). Lattice configurations included single (BCC, FCC, Cubic), dual-hybrid (Cubic+BCC, 
Cubic+FCC, BCC+FCC), and triple-hybrid (Cubic+BCC+FCC) combinations. To ensure a fair com-
parison, the total mass of all models was fixed at 27.0 g (19.78 g tube + 7.22 g lattice) by adjusting 
lattice strut diameters accordingly. Crashworthiness metrics (Total Energy Absorption (EA), Specific 
Energy Absorption (ES), Peak Crushing Force (FP), Mean Crushing Force (FM), and Crushing Force 
Efficiency (ηF)) were computed. Validation against published experimental data confirmed the accu-
racy of the FEA methodology, with a deviation percentage below 3.5%. Generally, the dual-hybrid 
and triple-hybrid models showed enhanced crashworthiness performance compared to single-hybrid 
models. The triple-hybrid model demonstrated the best crashworthiness performance with an EA of 
1024.009 J and an ES of 37.926 J/g. This represents a 13.5% improvement over the top dual-hybrid 
model and a 17.1% improvement over the best single-hybrid model.  The combination of multiple 
lattice structures within hybrid energy absorbers significantly improves crashworthiness performance. 
The findings support the integration of complex lattice architectures in lightweight energy-absorbing 
components for enhanced safety in transportation applications.

1. Introduction 
Thin-walled tubular structures are widely used as energy ab-
sorbers in various engineering applications, particularly in the 
automotive sector, where enhancing crash safety is crucial [1,2]. 
These components, which frequently serve as crash boxes, are 
designed to deform plastically upon collision, dissipating kinetic 
energy and reducing transmitted forces onto protected structures 
or passengers [3,4]. The research work in this field seeks to op-
timize these structures for maximal energy absorption, particu-
larly Specific Energy Absorption (𝐸𝑆), to facilitate lightweight 
design [5]. Besides, modification in the tube geometry, such as 
using multi-cell cross-sections (e.g. [6]), conical or tapered 
tubes (e.g. [7]), or incorporating surface features like corruga-
tions (e.g. [8]), can significantly influence the collapse mode and 
energy absorption characteristics under axial or oblique loading 
conditions. Material selection and distribution, such as using 
functionally graded materials or lightweight alloys like alumi-
num, also play a major important role  [9]. 
Filling the internal cavity of thin-walled tubes is an effective 
method for crashworthiness improvement. Whereas many stud-
ies have been conducted on metallic or polymeric foams as filler 
materials, which provided higher stability and absorbed energy

[10–12], recent developments in additive manufacturing (AM) 
have enabled the incorporation of more complex fillers, specifi-
cally lattice structures [13,14]. These lattice structures, com-
posed of interconnecting struts or surfaces, possess attractive 
properties like high specific strength and stiffness with a light-
weight, and their geometry can be tailored for specific mechan-
ical responses [15]. 
The concept of using lattices as fillers in thin-walled tubes has 
garnered significant interest. In the specialized area of crashwor-
thiness applications, Cetin and Baykasoğlu performed a pioneer-
ing study on the energy absorption behavior of lattice structure-
reinforced thin-walled tubes. The authors presented experi-
mental and numerical investigations on the crashworthiness ef-
fectiveness of square aluminum tubes filled with Body-Centered 
Cubic (BCC) and body-centered cubic with vertical strut (BCC-
Z) lattice structures under impact loading. Experiments indi-
cated that tubes filled with lattices exhibited much better energy 
absorption capacity and more stable crush behavior compared to 
empty tubes. More importantly, it was noted by the authors that 
the progressive collapse of lattice structures provided a con-
trolled resistance force during deformation, which resulted in 
improved overall crashworthiness metrics [16]. Tan et al. [3] 
proposed and investigated a novel auxetic hierarchical honey-
comb crash box for electric vehicles, combining hierarchical 
honeycombs and auxetic structures. This design showed excel-
lent energy absorption capabilities and was optimized using 
multi-objective algorithms, indicating its potential as a new so-
lution for enhancing vehicle crashworthiness.  
Kocabaş et al. [17] provided valuable experimental compari-
sons of energy absorption capacity between the thin-walled 
tubes filled with traditional (BCC and FCC) and novel hybrid 
(β-Ti3Au) lattice structures under identical test conditions. They 
concluded that hybrid lattice structures (β-Ti3Au), combining 
different unit cell topologies, often outperform single-topology 
lattices due to their complementary deformation mechanisms. 
Tao et al. [18] explored the crashworthiness of additively man-
ufactured lattice-reinforced thin-walled tube hybrid structures. 
They investigated the impact of varying cross-sectional cell 
numbers and gradient densities in BCC lattice-reinforced thin-
walled tubes, demonstrating significant increases in energy ab-
sorption and specific energy absorption compared to individual 
components and empty tubes. This study offers a method for op-
timizing impact resistance using experimental and numerical 
simulations. Subsequently, Tao et al. [19] focused on a BCC lat-
tice-filled thin-walled tube, comparing one-piece and split-
printed structures under axial and transverse compression. The 
one-piece structure showed superior performance in both defor-
mation mode and energy absorption, highlighting the potential 
of this hybrid design for lightweight and high-strength energy 
absorption. 
Wu et al. [20] investigated the dynamic mechanical properties 
and applications of advanced lattice structures in energy-absorb-
ing systems. The authors examined the dynamic mechanics of 
node-enhanced graded lattice structures, specifically the node-
enhanced body-centered cubic (NBCC) lattice, under dynamic 
impact. This research revealed that different gradient strategies 
influence energy absorption, with the vertical rod diameter gra-
dient NBCC (RGNBCC) being more effective for low-speed im-
pacts and the vertical height gradient NBCC (HGNBCC) for 
high-speed impacts, demonstrating the importance of tailoring 
lattice design to specific conditions. Bunsri et al. [15] took this 
field of research a step further by exploring the deformation be-
havior of crash boxes with truss-lattice and cellular structures. 
Their research compared different lattice structures, including 
BCC, Face-Centered Cubic (FCC), and Triply Periodic Minimal 
Surface (TPMS), which showed that the TPMS lattice structures 
had better energy absorption efficiency due to their better load 
distribution mechanisms. The authors emphasized the need to 
examine the interaction between the tube wall and the internal 
lattice during crushing because the behavior at this interface 
played a major role in the overall energy absorption behavior. 
Liu et al. [21] designed thin-walled tubes reinforced with alu-
minum gradient lattices manufactured via selective laser melting 
(SLM). They used both experimental drop-weight tests and fi-
nite element analysis to assess crashworthiness under low-speed 
impacts. The main findings were that inwardly graded lattices 
enhanced specific energy absorption by 17.44% over uniform 
lattices while maintaining stable deformation and peak force. 
Alam et al. [22] investigated metallic thin-walled tubes filled 
with Polyetherketoneketone (PEKK) bio-inspired hierarchical 
honeycomb lattices fabricated by fused deposition modeling 
(FDM). The authors demonstrated that a sparse hierarchical to-
pology improved specific energy absorption by over 202% com-
pared to hollow tubes, with further optimization achieved 
through cell rigidity and rib/wall thickness adjustments to bal-
ance energy absorption and peak load. Kandasamy and Ganesan 
explored polyamide (PA12) bi-tubular thin-walled tubes pro-
duced by selective laser sintering (SLS). They found that hybrid 
lattice-filled specimens exhibited up to 113.9% greater specific 
energy absorption than empty tubes and 42.8% more than uni-
form lattices. Moreover, their results highlighted the significant 
influence of lattice arrangement, wall thickness, and tube geom-
etry on crash response and structural stability [23]. 
Although considerable progress has been made in enhancing 
the crashworthiness performance of energy-absorbing structures 
using lattice-filled thin-walled tubes, most previous studies fo-
cused on single or gradient topologies. A systematic and com-
parative investigation of hybrid lattice combinations, particu-
larly under a unified FEA framework and identical mass con-
straints, remains limited. Furthermore, while additive manufac-
turing has made it feasible to fabricate complex geometries, the 
potential synergistic benefits of integrating dual- and triple-hy-
brid lattice structures within a single energy absorber have yet 
to be comprehensively explored. This represents a significant 
research gap, especially given the increasing demand for light-
weight, high-performance crashworthy systems in transporta-
tion and safety-critical applications.

To address this gap, the present study conducts a comprehen-

of hybrid thin-walled tube structures using Finite Element Anal-

filled with different lattice topologies: three single-lattice (BCC,

figuration. A constant total mass is maintained across all models 
by adjusting lattice strut diameters, enabling a fair and consistent 
performance comparison. The adopted FEA methodology is 
benchmarked against experimental results from the literature to 
ensure accuracy and reliability [16]. This study introduces a 
novel approach by systematically evaluating the influence of lat-
tice topology combinations on energy absorption, thereby offer-
ing new insights into the design of advanced crashworthy sys-
tems optimized through hybrid lattice integration. Figure 1

2.2. Finite Element Analysis 
FEA is a widely used method in the field of engineering 
[35,36]. FEA using Abaqus/Explicit serves as the primary sim-
ulation tool in this investigation. The FEA approach adopted in 
this study aligns closely with the validated methodologies pre-
sented in Ref [16], ensuring accuracy and consistency. Firstly, 
the three-dimensional hybrid models (thin-walled square tubes 
filled with single and hybrid lattice structures) were developed 
using PTC Creo Parametric 8, as illustrated in Figure 3. To ena-
ble a fair comparison of crashworthiness performance, a con-
stant total mass of 27.0 g was maintained for all models, con-
sisting of a 19.78 g thin-walled tube and 7.22 g of lattice struc-
ture. This was achieved by appropriately adjusting the lattice 
strut diameters. 
The external dimensions of the thin-walled square tubes were 
kept constant across all configurations, with a cross-section of 
20 × 20 mm², a wall thickness of 1.5 mm, and a length of 66 
mm. The tubes were filled with four unit cells of the respective 
lattice structures, each having a cross-section of 16.5 × 16.5 
mm². Al6063-T5 aluminum alloy was assigned to the empty 
tube, while AlSi10Mg aluminum alloy was assigned to all lattice 
structures. Both materials are modeled via an isotropic elastic–
plastic law with isotropic hardening ("Plasticity: Isotropic Hard-
ening"). By using the main mechanical properties and the stress-
strain data shown in Table 1 and Figure 2, respectively. Previous 
studies (e.g. [18]) indicate that for aluminum alloys, the influ-
ence of strain rate is negligible at compression rates up to 1 m/s. 
Thus, strain rate sensitivity and viscoplastic effects were not ac-
counted for.

The interactions between all components (rigid plates, thin-
walled tubes, and internal lattice structures) were defined using 
general contact properties. "Penalty" formulation with a friction 
coefficient of 0.25 was applied for the tangential direction be-
havior. This value was adopted from the experimentally vali-
dated reference study by Cetin & Baykasoğlu [16]. This penalty 
algorithm was chosen especially for its ability to handle general 
contact conditions, particularly with rigid bodies with many 
contact points per node. Whereas, a "hard contact" formulation 
was utilized for the normal direction behavior, to prevent unre-
alistic penetration between components during impact. To pre-
vent crushing structures from penetrating the rigid plates, the 
moving and fixed rigid plates were connected to the crushing 
structures by "tie" constraints using master-slave node relation-
ships. "Rigid body" constraints were defined for the moving and 
fixed rigid plates by picking all elements and linking them to the 
respective reference points (RP-1 in the moving plate and RP-2 
in the fixed plate). These constraints ensured that the entire plate 
acted as a single rigid body, with all degrees of freedom con-
trolled through the reference point. Interactions of the BCC hy-
brid FEA model are shown in Figure 5.

filled with various lattice structures (BCC, FCC, Cubic, and hy-

structure can absorb during the crushing process; it is propor-

Following the initial peak, each hybrid model showed distinct 
force-displacement behavior. The BCC hybrid model showed 
relatively consistent crushing force throughout the deformation 
process, with force values ranging between 16-22 kN during the 
plateau region. The FCC hybrid model showed similar plateau 
behavior with a force ranging between 16-21 kN, whereas the 
Cubic hybrid model had slightly lower force values but more 
stable crushing behavior. Plateau region refers to the portion of 
the load-displacement curve after the initial peak force, where 
the force sustained by the structure remains relatively constant 
or oscillates around an average value as the deformation (dis-
placement) increases [26].  
The crushing displacement (𝛿) used for calculating the crash-
worthiness metrics was determined to correspond to the effec-
tive crushing distance for each structure. This distance is meas-
ured up to the point of densification, where the structure is fully 
compacted and the crushing force rises dramatically following 
the plateau region. The densification point was determined from 
the force-displacement curve as roughly 47.5 mm for the empty 
tube. Whereas the densification point was determined as roughly 
42.5 mm for all hybrid models to ensure a fair comparison and 
physically significant evaluation of their total energy absorption 
capacity. Since the empty tube and the various lattice-filled 
tubes have different internal structures and crushing behaviors, 
their effective crushing distances before densification are not 
identical. Table 3 compares the FEA crashworthiness metrics 
values of the empty tube and hybrid models at the displacement 
of roughly 47.5 and 42.5mm, respectively. Generally, all hybrid 
models showed enhanced crashworthiness performance com-
pared to the empty tube. 
The BCC hybrid model provided the highest energy absorp-
tion capacity (874.267 J) and specific energy absorption (32.380 
J/g) among the single-hybrid models. The BCC lattice struc-
tures' superior performance is due to their diagonal struts, which 
facilitate efficient multi-directional load transfer and sequential 
layer-by-layer collapse. These struts primarily undergo com-
bined axial-bending deformation modes, leading to more stable 
progressive collapse mechanisms and consequently higher en-
ergy absorption [27,28]. The FCC hybrid model showed inter-
mediate energy absorption (856.612 J) with a specific energy 
absorption of 31.726 J/g. FCC lattices typically exhibit higher 
nodal connectivity than BCC structures, providing greater initial 
stiffness but potentially less progressive collapse behavior 
[29,30]. The Cubic hybrid model showed the lowest energy ab-
sorption (816.400 J), however exhibited the highest crush force 
efficiency (0.685) among the single lattice structures. This char-
acteristic behavior can be explained by the Cubic lattice's or-
thogonal strut arrangement, which produces more uniform 
crushing behavior aligned with principal loading directions. 
While this architectural regularity leads to more consistent force 
levels during deformation (resulting in higher crush force effi-
ciency), the smaller number of struts participating in energy dis-
sipation compared to the spatially distributed BCC and FCC ar-
rangements limits its total energy absorption capacity [31,32].  
For the dual-hybrid models, the Cubic+BCC hybrid model 
exhibited an improved load-carrying capacity during the plateau 
region compared to the single-hybrid models, with a mean 
crushing force of 20.874 kN and energy absorption of 885.348 
J. Also, the Cubic+FCC hybrid model showed enhanced perfor-
mance with a mean crushing force of 20.786 kN and energy ab-
sorption of 883.335 J. The BCC+FCC hybrid model showed sig-
nificant improvement, with the highest energy absorption 
(902.134 J) and specific energy absorption (33.412 J/g) among 
the dual hybrid models. However, this model also exhibited the 
lowest crush force efficiency (0.521) among all hybrid models, 
indicating larger fluctuations between peak and mean crushing 
forces. 
The triple-hybrid model, which combines all three lattice 
types (Cubic+BCC+FCC), showed the most favorable crash-
worthiness behavior among all hybrid models. This model pro-
vided the highest energy absorption (1024.009 J) and the highest 
specific energy absorption (37.926 J/g) among all hybrid mod-
els, representing a 13.5% improvement over the best-performing 
dual hybrid model (BCC+FCC hybrid) and a 17.1% increase 
over the best-performing single-hybrid model (BCC hybrid). 
The triple-hybrid model maintained a mean crushing force of 
24.097 kN with a relatively moderate crush force efficiency of 
0.563. Though this efficiency is not as high as that of the Cubic 
hybrid model (0.685), the triple-hybrid model's significantly 
higher energy absorption capacity makes it the superior overall

where the combination of different topologies creates structures 
with mutually reinforcing collapse patterns and load paths [33]. 
Furthermore, multi-topology lattice structures typically exhibit 
multi-stage collapse behavior where different lattice compo-
nents activate at various strain levels. This sequential activation 
of deformation mechanisms extends the plateau region and in-
creases the total energy absorption through more effective ma-
terial utilization [34]. Figure 10 shows the comparison of de-
formed shapes of the empty tube and hybrid models under axial 
impact loading at a displacement of 25mm.

These results highlight important design trade-offs for engi-
neering applications. For applications requiring high force sta-
bility, such as components protecting sensitive equipment, the 
Cubic hybrid is a strong applicant due to its exceptional crush 
force efficiency (𝜂𝐹 = 0.685). For applications where maximiz-
ing total energy dissipation in a lightweight package is signifi-
cant, such as automotive crash boxes, the triple-hybrid model is 
the superior choice. It's significantly higher specific energy ab-
sorption (𝐸𝑆 = 37.926 J/g) makes it the most effective at absorb-
ing impact energy for a given mass, even though its force profile 
is less uniform than the Cubic hybrid's. 
4. Conclusions 
This study successfully investigated the crashworthiness per-
formance of thin-walled tubes filled with single, dual-hybrid, 
and triple-hybrid lattice structures using a validated FEA ap-
proach. Based on the thorough analysis of the findings, the fol-
lowing conclusions can be drawn: 
 
The FEA methodology, benchmarked against published ex-
perimental results, was confirmed to be reliable, validating 
the comparative analysis across the different hybrid models. 
 
Combining multiple lattice topologies within a single filler 
structure provides significant synergistic benefits. The pro-
gressive increase in mean crushing force from single-hybrid 
(up to 20.6 kN) to dual-hybrid (up to 21.2 kN) and finally 
to the triple-hybrid model (24.1 kN) clearly demonstrates 
the reinforcing effects of integrating different collapse 
mechanisms. 
 
The triple-hybrid structure stands out as the most effective 
overall design for crashworthiness. Its superior energy ab-
sorption is not just an additive effect but stems from a com-
plex interaction between the different lattice types, leading 
to more efficient material utilization and an extended, high-
force plateau region during crushing. Therefore, it can be 
ideal for applications where maximizing total energy dissi-
pation in a lightweight package is significant, such as auto-
motive crash boxes. 
 
A clear trade-off exists between maximum energy absorp-
tion and crushing stability. While the BCC-based structures 
excelled at energy dissipation, the orthogonal Cubic struc-
ture provided the most uniform crushing force, making it 
ideal for applications requiring high crush force efficiency, 
such as components protecting sensitive equipment.  
The findings of this study are based on FEA. Therefore, ex-
perimental validation of the novel dual- and triple-hybrid con-
figurations is a critical next step to confirm the predicted perfor-
mance enhancements. Future research should also expand the 
scope to include more complex loading conditions, such as 
oblique and transverse impacts, which are common in real-
world crash scenarios. Finally, employing multi-objective opti-
mization algorithms could help to further refine these hybrid de-
signs and explore a broader range of performance trade-offs.
